lessons: Check the source date before using a fact.
Separate observed facts from personal interpretation.
State the investment question in one sentence.
Record the evidence available at review time.
Prefer primary sources when they are available.
Note when a figure is estimated rather than reported.
Compare like periods before drawing a conclusion.
Use consistent units across every comparison.
Reconcile headline figures with underlying details.
Treat missing data as uncertainty, not reassurance.
Identify which assumptions drive the conclusion.
Test the conclusion against a reasonable alternative.
Write down what would change your view.
Distinguish temporary effects from lasting changes.
Review both the upside and the downside case.
Check whether growth relies on a narrow base.
Separate revenue growth from price increases.
Examine cash generation alongside reported profit.
Compare capital spending with maintenance needs.
Review debt terms, not only the debt total.
Check when major obligations come due.
Consider dilution when evaluating per-share value.
Track changes in share count over time.
Review working capital for unusual movements.
Compare margins on a consistent basis.
Look for one-time items in adjusted results.
Verify whether adjustments recur frequently.
Check whether accounting choices changed.
Read footnotes before relying on summary tables.
Compare guidance with prior reporting habits.
Note where management has limited visibility.
Separate management targets from achieved figures.
Examine incentives behind key decisions.
Check whether compensation matches long-term goals.
Review related-party dealings with care.
Look for changes in auditors or reporting controls.
Assess whether governance supports accountability.
Consider how concentrated decision authority is.
Check whether succession plans are credible.
Review insider ownership without assuming alignment.
Define the relevant customer before sizing demand.
Distinguish market size from reachable demand.
Check whether customer concentration is material.
Review customer retention using consistent definitions.
Separate new demand from replacement demand.
Consider how easily customers can switch.
Identify the main reason customers choose the product.
Test whether pricing power is supported by evidence.
Review sales efficiency across comparable periods.
Check whether channel partners create dependency.
Identify the strongest source of competitive pressure.
Avoid treating popularity as a durable advantage.
Ask what prevents a capable rival from copying.
Review whether scale improves unit economics.
Separate network effects from simple market growth.
Check whether intellectual property is enforceable.
Consider the cost of maintaining the competitive edge.
Review supplier concentration and alternatives.
Identify dependencies on scarce inputs.
Check whether contracts protect key relationships.
Evaluate management execution against stated plans.
Compare capital allocation with declared priorities.
Review acquisitions using original objectives.
Separate organic progress from acquired growth.
Check whether integration costs are fully counted.
Consider whether buybacks offset dilution.
Review dividends against free cash capacity.
Assess whether reinvestment returns are measurable.
Look for evidence of disciplined project selection.
Check whether expansion increases operational complexity.
Define the valuation method before choosing inputs.
Use more than one reasonable valuation approach.
Keep discount rates consistent with the risk case.
Avoid false precision in long-range forecasts.
Use ranges when uncertainty is meaningful.
Compare valuation with normalized economics.
Separate cyclical peaks from sustainable earnings.
Check whether terminal assumptions dominate value.
Test sensitivity to margins and growth.
Include financing needs in the valuation.
Match currency assumptions across the analysis.
Account for taxes in cash flow estimates.
Distinguish enterprise value from equity value.
Include off-balance-sheet obligations where relevant.
Compare multiples using consistent definitions.
Avoid relying on a single comparable.
Review liquidity before considering position size.
Match position size to evidence quality.
Consider downside before expected return.
Define loss limits before taking risk.
Avoid concentration that exceeds conviction.
Check correlations during stressed conditions.
Separate business risk from portfolio risk.
Consider currency exposure explicitly.
Review interest-rate sensitivity where relevant.
Identify regulatory dependencies.
Consider legal risks without predicting court decisions.
Review operational risks and recovery plans.
Check whether insurance covers material exposures.
Treat geopolitical exposure as a scenario, not a forecast.
Record the original thesis before updating it.
Date every material change to the thesis.
Update assumptions when new evidence arrives.
Avoid changing the standard after seeing results.
Compare actual developments with prior expectations.
Distinguish a weak thesis from poor timing.
Do not let purchase price define intrinsic value.
Review contrary evidence before confirming a view.
Seek disconfirming facts with equal effort.
Keep confidence proportional to evidence quality.
Note unresolved questions explicitly.
Assign an owner and date to follow-up work.
Preserve links to supporting sources.
Summarize the key risk in plain language.
State the time horizon for each claim.
Separate monitoring signals from decision rules.
Review the thesis on a regular schedule.
Close stale questions that no longer matter.
Document why a decision was deferred.
End each review with a clear next check.
